back: A measure of the organisation's financial performance based primarily on data from the financial reporting system.

Quantitative = expressed in numbers (vs. qualitative: smileys, arrows). Financial indicators are always quantitative, but there are quantitative non-financial indicators (defects, satisfaction rate, absenteeism).

1) Activity
2) Profitability
3) Return on investment
4) Value creation
5) Cash flow
Turnover, growth rate – ability to generate revenue.
Net income, operating income, NOPAT, EBIT, operating profit margin, EBITDA – capacity to generate revenues exceeding costs.
ROE, ROCE – profitability relative to the capital invested to obtain the income.
MVA, TSR, EVA – compare financial performance with the return required for the risk of investing in the organisation.
EBITDA, operating cash flow, NCF – financing needs or capacity to generate cash.
Ability of a company to generate income in excess of the cost of the resources consumed (positive income / profit).

Ability to generate sufficient profit relative to the capital used.
ROE: shareholders' view (return on equity).
ROCE: managers' / operating view.
Ability to offer investors a return above the opportunity cost of their investment in the company.
ROI = operating profit margin × asset turnover (sales / capital employed) – the two levers of return on investment.
The ratio formalism and the valuation of capital in the denominator can generate decision biases.
Complex to build; problems of implementation, comparison, interpretation. Market values also reflect macro-sectoral / macro-economic expectations.
More comprehensive indicators are more valid but often less reliable → a compromise must be found.
